scope: Agent interoperability protocols (MCP, A2A, AG-UI/CopilotKit, OTel GenAI, OpenAI Realtime, 2026 registries) — mechanisms a Hermes plugin harness must implement to be cross-native (cross-protocol, cross-surface, cross-provider).
unreachable: https://open-json-ui.org/ — fetch blocked ('URL targets a private or internal network address'); no authoritative OpenAI Open-JSON-UI spec page reachable. Do not implement against a guessed schema; A2UI (v0.9.1) and MCP Apps are the reachable declarative-UI specs.

https://docs.copilotkit.ai/coagents/generative-ui/agentic — returned a client-side error shell ('This page couldn't load'); the current generative-UI docs live under /langgraph-python/* and the v2 reference tree.
https://docs.copilotkit.ai/reference/hooks/useCoAgent — URL now serves the useAgent reference. useCoAgent has been superseded by useAgent in the v2 SDK.

patterns.name: tools/list + tools/call with cursor pagination and capability negotiation
patterns.what: Server declares capabilities.tools (optionally listChanged) in the initialize response. Client discovers via tools/list (supports `cursor` -> `nextCursor` pagination) and invokes via tools/call with params {name, arguments}. Tool results carry `content` (text/image/audio/resource blocks) and an `isError` boolean; unknown tool is JSON-RPC -32602, unknown method -32601. Lifecycle: client MUST send `notifications/initialized` after the initialize response before normal traffic; on HTTP every subsequent request MUST carry `MCP-Protocol-Version: <version>`.
patterns.why: This is the only mechanism by which a Hermes plugin can enumerate and invoke tools from an arbitrary MCP server. hermes-day currently treats tool calls as opaque hook payloads (pre_tool_call/post_tool_call) with no server-side discovery, so it cannot present a server's real tool surface in the cockpit, and cannot tell 'tool not found' from 'tool errored'.
patterns.build: New module `hday_protocols.py` with `MCPClient` class: `initialize()` -> capability dict, `list_tools()` draining cursors, `call_tool(name, arguments, _meta=None)`. Emit a normalized `ToolDescriptor{server, name, title, description, input_schema, annotations}` and a `ToolResult{is_error, content_blocks, server, duration_ms}`. Feed both into the existing gate ledger (`hday_gate.py` decision records gain `server`, `tool`, `jsonrpc_id`). Desktop: `desktop/plugin.js` gains a `mcp.tools` panel section rendering ToolDescriptor rows with an `isError` chip. Never conflate -32602/-32601 with a tool's own isError=true.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_tools.py — fixture JSON-RPC server (in-process, stdio and HTTP modes) that returns two pages of tools/list with nextCursor, a -32602 for an unknown tool, and an isError=true tool result. Assert: cursor drained exactly once, ToolDescriptor count == expected, isError surfaced separately from JSON-RPC errors, MCP-Protocol-Version header present on every HTTP request.

patterns.name: Resources: URI-addressed context, templates, subscribe/list_changed
patterns.what: resources/list (paginated), resources/templates/list for RFC 6570 URI templates, resources/read -> contents[] of {uri, mimeType, text} or {uri, mimeType, blob(base64)}. Capability `resources:{subscribe?, listChanged?}` — both optional and independent. Subscribed URIs push `notifications/resources/updated`; list mutations push `notifications/resources/list_changed`. Missing resource is -32002. Standard schemes: https://, file://, git://; custom schemes MUST follow RFC 3986. Resources are application-driven (host decides inclusion), unlike prompts which are user-driven.
patterns.why: Resources are how an external server contributes context that hermes-day's context scorer should be able to see and rank. Today `hday_ctxscore.py` scores only Hermes-native context; a server-backed resource (a repo's config, a schema, a live dashboard) is invisible to it. Subscribe/list_changed is also the correct push primitive for 'the world changed, re-score'.
patterns.build: In `hday_protocols.py`: `list_resources()`, `list_resource_templates()`, `read_resource(uri) -> ResourceContent{uri, mime_type, text|blob_b64, size}`. Add `ResourceSubscriber` that issues resources/subscribe and routes `notifications/resources/updated` into `hday_ctxscore.py` as an invalidation event (re-score that URI's contribution, do not full-recompute). Handle -32002 as `ResourceGone` and drop the cache entry. Desktop: resource reads render in the existing terminal block style; blob content shows size + mime only, never inline base64.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_resources.py — server advertises resources:{subscribe:true,listChanged:false} only; assert the client does not expect list_changed, that reading a missing URI raises ResourceGone (not a generic error), and that a resources/updated notification triggers exactly one ctxscore invalidation for that URI and zero for others.

patterns.name: Prompts as user-invoked slash commands with typed arguments
patterns.what: prompts/list returns {name, title, description, arguments[{name, description, required}]} with pagination; prompts/get takes {name, arguments{}} and returns messages[] whose content is one of text, image (base64+mimeType), audio (base64+mimeType), or an embedded `resource` block. Arguments can be auto-completed through the completion utility. Capability `prompts:{listChanged?}`. Invalid name / missing required arg is -32602. The spec's own interaction model is a slash command in the client UI.
patterns.why: Prompts are the one MCP primitive the spec explicitly marks user-controlled — exactly the shape of a cockpit's quick-action rail. hermes-day already has a command surface (keyboard triage: a/d/s/o) and a filter field; MCP prompts give it a server-supplied, argument-typed action vocabulary without hermes-day hardcoding any workflow.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `list_prompts()`, `get_prompt(name, arguments)` -> `PromptInvocation{messages[], description}`. Map each prompt to a cockpit action: `desktop/plugin.js` filter field gains `:` prefix routing (e.g. `:code_review`) that opens an argument form generated from `arguments[]` (required ones block submit). Render returned messages through the same card pipeline as sessions, tagging the card with the owning server. Cache prompt lists with TTL; honour prompts/list_changed by invalidating.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_prompts.py — assert required-argument enforcement happens client-side before any RPC is sent, that an embedded resource block survives round-trip without base64 corruption, that -32602 from prompts/get surfaces as a form-validation error (not a crash), and that list_changed invalidates the cached list exactly once.

patterns.name: Roots: client-declared filesystem scope + list_changed
patterns.what: Client declares capability `roots:{listChanged:true}`. Server issues a `roots/list` request; client answers `{roots:[{uri:'file:///abs/path', name:'Display'}]}` — uri MUST be a file:// URI in this revision, name optional. On change the client MUST send `notifications/roots/list_changed`. Unsupported -> -32601; internal error -> -32603. Clients MUST validate root URIs to prevent path traversal and MUST only expose roots with appropriate permissions; servers SHOULD validate all paths against provided roots. NOTE: SEP-2577 deprecates roots in the 2026-07-28 revision.
patterns.why: Roots are the protocol-level expression of 'which directories is this agent allowed to touch' — precisely the boundary hermes-day's honesty guard polices when it vetoes test-file deletion and exit-code laundering. Binding that guard to a declared root set turns a heuristic veto into a scope check, and gives the cockpit a truthful blast-radius column.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `RootProvider` with `set_roots(list[Path])` (normalizes to file:// absolute URIs, rejects symlink escapes and any path outside configured workspaces), `handle_roots_list()`, and `notify_roots_changed()`. Wire into `hday_gate.py`: every pre_tool_call decision record gains `in_scope: bool` computed against the active root set; out-of-scope writes escalate rather than auto-approve. Desktop: the escalation matrix panel shows the root set and per-root write counts. Implement roots as the *legacy* path behind a version check — see mcp2026-stateless-discover.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_roots.py — assert path traversal (`file:///workspace/../../etc`) is rejected, that a root removal emits exactly one list_changed, that in_scope is false for a path outside all roots and the gate escalates instead of allowing, and that a client without the capability answers roots/list with -32601.

patterns.name: Sampling + elicitation: the two server->client reverse requests (and MRTR in 2026)
patterns.what: Sampling: server sends `sampling/createMessage` with messages[], systemPrompt, maxTokens, optional modelPreferences; client returns CreateMessageResult {role, content, model, stopReason}. Elicitation: server sends `elicitation/create` with {mode:'form', message, requestedSchema (JSON Schema object)}; client returns ElicitResult {action:'accept'|'decline'|'cancel', content}. Both are client capabilities (`sampling:{}`, `elicitation:{}`). In 2026-07-28 both are *replaced* by Multi Round-Trip Requests: the server returns InputRequiredResult {resultType:'input_required', inputRequests:{key:{method,params}}, requestState?} and the client retries the ORIGINAL request with inputResponses keyed identically, a NEW JSON-RPC id, and requestState echoed byte-for-byte and never inspected. Server-initiated requests are no longer supported.
patterns.why: These are the protocol-level human-in-the-loop channels: a remote server asking *this* agent's user a question. hermes-day's entire thesis is triaging everything waiting on you across profiles — but it has no notion of a third-party protocol asking. Implementing both shapes (legacy server-initiated and MRTR) is what makes the cockpit cross-native without a per-server adapter.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `ReverseRequestRouter` that classifies an inbound server request as {sampling, elicitation, mrtr_input_required} and converts it into a cockpit card of kind 'question' with a typed answer form built from requestedSchema. On answer, produce ElicitResult / CreateMessageResult (legacy) or the inputResponses retry (MRTR) — same card, two wire encodings. MRTR contract enforced in code: `request_state_echo` is stored as an opaque bytes blob, asserted equal on retry, and explicitly NOT parsed. Sampling requests MUST route through the gate: a server must not silently spend this profile's model budget.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mrtr.py — (a) legacy path: server-initiated elicitation becomes a card and the accept/decline/cancel triple maps to the right ElicitResult actions; (b) MRTR path: requestState round-trips byte-identical, the retry carries a different JSON-RPC id, a tampered requestState is rejected by the fixture server, and a partial inputResponses map is answered with a fresh InputRequiredResult rather than an error; (c) a sampling request without gate approval never reaches the provider.

patterns.name: Streamable HTTP transport + OAuth 2.1 resource-server authorization
patterns.what: One HTTP endpoint (e.g. POST /mcp) handling all JSON-RPC. Client POSTs with `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`; the server replies either a single JSON response or an SSE stream carrying the response plus any interleaved server requests/notifications. Session management via `Mcp-Session-Id` returned on initialize and echoed thereafter. `MCP-Protocol-Version: <version>` header required on all requests after initialization. Shutdown = closing the HTTP connection. Authorization: the MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 *resource server*; it publishes RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata and returns 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="<url>"`, which drives discovery of the authorization server.
patterns.why: Remote MCP servers are the cross-provider half of 'cross-native'. Without a transport that multiplexes server->client requests onto a response stream, the reverse-request patterns above are unreachable over HTTP; without resource-metadata discovery, every server needs bespoke auth wiring. hermes-day's vault panel already tracks per-source credentials — this is the standard that lets it do so generically.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `StreamableHTTPTransport` — POST with the required Accept header, parse both `application/json` and `text/event-stream` replies from the same code path, persist Mcp-Session-Id per server, attach MCP-Protocol-Version, and demultiplex SSE frames into {response, server_request, notification}. On 401, parse `resource_metadata` from WWW-Authenticate, fetch the PRM document, and surface an auth card in the vault panel with the discovered authorization server + scopes; never store the token in the plugin config.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_streamable_http.py — fixture server that (a) replies JSON to one request and SSE to the next on the same endpoint, (b) interleaves a server->client sampling request inside an SSE response, (c) returns 401 + WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata on a missing token. Assert the demultiplexer routes each frame correctly, that a missing MCP-Protocol-Version header is a hard client-side error, and that a token is never written into the plugin's on-disk config.

patterns.name: 2026 stateless MCP: server/discover + per-request _meta, no initialize handshake
patterns.what: The initialize/notifications-initialized handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are REMOVED. Every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in `params._meta`: `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`. Servers SHOULD identify themselves in each result's `_meta` under `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`. `server/discover` MUST be implemented by servers and returns {resultType:'complete', supportedVersions:[...], capabilities:{...}, instructions?, ttlMs, cacheScope, _meta:{...serverInfo}}; it is cacheable. Version mismatch -> `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`. On stdio, `server/discover` doubles as the backward-compatibility probe against legacy handshake servers. serverInfo is self-reported, unverified, and MUST NOT drive security decisions.
patterns.why: This is the single biggest 2026 change and it inverts the harness design: a client can no longer assume a session exists, and capability truth lives per-request rather than in one handshake. A harness that keeps an initialize-shaped cache will silently mis-negotiate against 2026 servers. It is also what makes MCP servers safe behind ordinary stateless HTTP load balancers — the deployment shape most remote Hermes profiles will use.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `MCPNegotiator` that (1) calls server/discover first, (2) caches DiscoverResult keyed by server with `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` respected, (3) falls back to the legacy initialize handshake when discover fails on stdio, and (4) stamps every outgoing request's `_meta` with protocolVersion + clientCapabilities + clientInfo. Capability checks read from the per-request stamped set, never from a module-global. Record the negotiated version in the gate ledger so a post-hoc audit can tell which protocol revision a decision was made under.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp2026_discover.py — assert discover is called exactly once per TTL window (not per request), that a 2026 server never receives an initialize request, that a legacy stdio server is detected and driven through the handshake fallback, that an unsupported version raises UnsupportedProtocolVersionError rather than degrading silently, and that serverInfo never appears in any authorization decision.

patterns.name: subscriptions/listen: one long-lived stream with a negotiated notification filter
patterns.what: Replaces the HTTP GET endpoint and resources/subscribe|unsubscribe. Client sends `subscriptions/listen` with params.notifications = {toolsListChanged?:bool, promptsListChanged?:bool, resourcesListChanged?:bool, resourceSubscriptions?:[uri]} — all optional, omitted means not subscribed. Server MUST send `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged` as the FIRST message, carrying `_meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId']` (the JSON-RPC id of the listen request) and the subset it agreed to honour, and MUST NOT send anything on that subscription before it. Every subsequent notification carries the same subscriptionId. Multiple concurrent subscriptions are allowed and demultiplexed by that id. Graceful closure = a normal completion response to the original listen request; an abrupt transport close is a reconnect trigger, and on stdio the client MUST re-send subscriptions/listen after reconnect (no server-side subscription state survives).
patterns.why: This is the push spine of the cockpit. hermes-day's 'Needs you' / 'In flight' sections currently poll Hermes-native session state; a negotiated notification stream is how a remote server's tool-list churn or resource changes become live cockpit updates instead of stale rows. The acknowledged-subset handshake also lets the UI be honest about what it will and won't be told.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `SubscriptionStream` with `open(filter) -> SubscriptionId`, an `acknowledged` gate (no notification is dispatched before ack is seen), per-subscriptionId dispatch table, and reconnect logic that re-sends the exact original filter. Map toolsListChanged -> invalidate the mcp.tools panel cache; resourceSubscriptions -> ctxscore invalidation; promptsListChanged -> prompt cache. Desktop: a source row shows `subscribed: 2/3 types` from the acknowledged filter, so a server silently dropping a type is visible.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp2026_subscriptions.py — assert a notification arriving before acknowledged is dropped and logged (not dispatched), that two concurrent subscriptions on one stdio channel demultiplex correctly by subscriptionId, that a server dropping resourcesListChanged from the ack results in the UI showing 2/3 rather than a hang, and that after a simulated transport drop the client re-sends the identical filter.

patterns.name: Extension negotiation: `extensions` capability maps + graceful degradation
patterns.what: Extensions are identified as `{vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}`, e.g. `io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials`, `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`. Clients advertise support inside `_meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities'].extensions` on every request (each extension's settings object is its own schema; `{}` = no settings); servers advertise theirs in the `server/discover` response under `capabilities.extensions`. Official extensions live in modelcontextprotocol/ext-* repos; experimental ones in experimental-ext-* tied to a working group. The rules: an extension MUST NOT remove/rename fields, change types, alter existing semantics, or add new required fields; unsupported peers must get core-protocol fallback or an explicit error if the extension is mandatory.
patterns.why: This is the extension point that makes 'cross-native' additive rather than forked. Everything valuable in 2026 MCP (Apps, Tasks, Skills, auth flows) ships as an extension, so a harness that hardcodes core-only will look compatible while quietly missing every interactive capability. The no-breaking-changes rule is also a testable contract a harness can assert against.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `ExtensionRegistry` mapping identifier -> {client_settings, server_settings, mandatory: bool, fallback: callable}. Stamp the client's supported set into every request `_meta`. Add `hday_manifest.py` awareness: the plugin's own manifest gains a `protocol_extensions` block so a deployment can declare which extensions it requires, and startup fails loudly if a required extension is absent rather than degrading. Desktop: the service-wall panel shows per-server extension support as chips.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_extensions.py — assert the client's extensions map is present on every outgoing request (including ones unrelated to the extension), that a mandatory-but-unsupported extension produces an explicit startup error, that a non-mandatory one degrades to core behavior, and that a third-party prefix not matching `{reverse-dns}/{name}` is rejected at registration.

patterns.name: MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui): sandboxed interactive UI inside tool results
patterns.what: An official extension (repo modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps) letting a server return interactive UI inline in a conversation. MVP is HTML-only, addressed by MIME type `text/html;profile=mcp-app`; clients declare support as `extensions: {'io.modelcontextprotocol/ui': {mimeTypes: ['text/html;profile=mcp-app']}}`. UI runs in a sandboxed iframe with restricted permissions; UI-to-host communication is JSON-RPC (loggable/auditable), not a global API object; hosts may predeclare/review templates; UI-initiated tool calls can require explicit user consent. An `externalIframes` capability exists for external-URL content (deferred from the MVP). Rejected alternatives: a custom message protocol, and a host-injected global API object (breaks with external iframe sources).
patterns.why: This is the highest-leverage cross-surface item in the cluster: it is how a remote server ships a real widget (chart, form, video, diff view) into hermes-day's rail without hermes-day shipping code for it. It is also the only generative-UI mechanism that is already an official MCP extension with a defined trust model — directly relevant because hermes-day's cockpit already renders untrusted command output.
patterns.build: `desktop/plugin.js`: an `mcp.app` card type that renders an iframe with `sandbox` set (no allow-same-origin), srcdoc from the predeclared template, `postMessage`-based JSON-RPC bridge, and a hard allowlist of UI->host methods (at minimum: tool-call request, resize, log). Every UI-initiated tool call routes through `hday_gate.py` as its own decision record with `origin: 'mcp-app'` and requires explicit consent by default. Advertise the extension in the client capability map. Never execute UI-provided HTML outside the sandbox and never let it read plugin state directly.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_apps.py + a node:vm/jsdom harness for plugin.js — assert the iframe is created with sandbox lacking allow-same-origin, that an unlisted postMessage method is dropped, that a UI-initiated tool call produces a gate decision record with origin='mcp-app' and is denied without consent, and that a tool result without the extension falls back to plain text rendering.

patterns.name: Tasks extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks): polling, mid-flight input, durable handles
patterns.what: Long-running operations as first-class async: a server MAY return a task handle unsolicited (no per-request opt-in, unlike 2025-11-25), clients poll with `tasks/get`, send input with `tasks/update`, and cancel with `tasks/cancel`. `tasks/result` is REMOVED (clients calling it MUST receive -32601), `tasks/list` is REMOVED, and the `task` parameter on CallToolRequest is removed (servers MUST ignore it). Results are polymorphic — a plain CallToolResult and a task handle are both valid for any augmented request, and a client that negotiated the extension MUST handle both. Task IDs MAY be bearer tokens for server-side state and MUST be unguessable. Authz MUST be re-checked on every task-related request. Removing tasks/list is an explicit anti-leak measure: no cross-caller task enumeration.
patterns.why: Hermes agents routinely run jobs that outlive a turn. Today that state lives only in Hermes sessions; a remote server's task is a parallel, invisible world. Absorbing MCP task handles into the cockpit's 'In flight' / 'Scheduled' sections is what makes the day view complete rather than Hermes-only, and the unguessable-ID + per-request-authz rules are directly assertable in the harness.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `TaskHandle{task_id, server, created_at, status, last_polled}`; `poll_task()` with backoff, `update_task()`, `cancel_task()`. A task handle arriving where a tool result was expected is detected by shape (polymorphic result) and registered as an in-flight item rather than rendered as a tool result. Desktop: tasks render in the In-flight section with a distinct source chip and a cancel affordance. Never persist task IDs in a place that leaks them into logs; treat them as secrets in the ledger.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_tasks.py — assert a polymorphic result (handle where a CallToolResult was expected) registers an in-flight item and does not error; that tasks/result is never called and -32601 is handled; that a task ID is redacted from log output; that tasks/list is never used for discovery; and that a second profile cannot enumerate another profile's tasks.

patterns.name: Skills over MCP (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills): serving Agent Skills as resources
patterns.what: Serves Agent Skills (the agentskills.io SKILL.md format) over MCP: discovery via `skills/list` and retrieval via `skills/get`, with supporting files exposed as MCP resources, directory listing via `resources/directory/read` (including a 'held entry' concept for directory reads), and per-skill `_meta` key conventions. Skills can nest. A pointer can be exposed from server `instructions`. Files are retrieved lazily as needed, so cost scales with files actually used, not skill size. An archive form was considered and deferred (symlink/executable-bit and host-unpacking risk).
patterns.why: hermes-day is itself a plugin with a skill-shaped surface, and Hermes already has a skills system. A remote server offering skills over MCP is a direct extension of the harness's own mental model — and the lazy-retrieval design means the cockpit can list a server's skills without paying for their contents. This is also the mechanism that lets one profile lend a skill to another.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `list_skills()`, `get_skill(name)`, `read_skill_resource(uri)`. Represent each remote skill as a first-class entry in `hday_manifest.py` with `origin: 'mcp:<server>'` so local and remote skills are uniformly listable and a name collision is detectable. Desktop: an extension of the existing panel list showing remote skills with their server chip and a 'pull' action. Do NOT auto-execute or auto-install a remote skill; retrieval is explicit.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_mcp_skills.py — assert a remote skill and a local skill with the same name are both listed and flagged as a collision rather than one silently winning; that skill files are fetched only when read (count RPCs); and that nested skills resolve their own resources under the right parent.

patterns.name: Agent Card discovery: well-known URI, skills, capabilities, signatures, caching
patterns.what: The Agent Card is a JSON 'business card' describing: identity (name, description, provider), service endpoint (`url`), A2A capabilities (`streaming`, `pushNotifications`, and — after the v1.0 move — `extendedAgentCard`), authentication `schemes` (e.g. Bearer, OAuth2), and skills as AgentSkill objects {id, name, description, inputModes, outputModes, examples}. Three discovery strategies: (1) well-known URI, (2) curated registries / catalog-based, (3) direct configuration / private. Cards may be signed (RFC 7515 JWS + RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization) and clients should verify. Servers should send Cache-Control/max-age and an ETag derived from the card's `version` field or a content hash; clients should use If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since rather than unconditional re-fetch. Sensitive cards are protected by mTLS, IP restrictions, OAuth, or registry selective disclosure — never by embedded static secrets. `GetExtendedAgentCard` retrieves an authenticated, session-scoped extended card.
patterns.why: A2A is the peer-to-peer axis of cross-native: hermes-day triages across profiles and connections, and a remote agent is a new kind of source. The card is the only standard way to learn what a remote agent can do, and the signature + caching rules decide whether the cockpit can trust and cheaply refresh that knowledge. Extended Agent Card also gives a clean split between public and authenticated capability disclosure.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `AgentCardClient` — fetch the well-known card, verify a JWS signature when present (reject unsigned when policy demands it), honour ETag/max-age, and call GetExtendedAgentCard when authenticated. Normalize into `RemoteAgent{id, name, provider, url, skills[], streaming, push_notifications, auth_schemes, card_version, signature_verified}`. `hday_router.py` uses skills[] + inputModes/outputModes to route a task to a remote agent instead of a local profile. Desktop: remote agents appear in the Sources section with a `signed` / `unsigned` chip and a card-age indicator.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_card.py — fixture cards covering: unsigned, validly signed, tampered-payload (must fail verification), and one with an ETag that yields 304. Assert a tampered card is rejected, that a 304 does not re-download the body, that skills/inputModes drive router selection, and that no credential from the card is ever written to disk.

patterns.name: A2A task lifecycle: contextId/taskId, eight TaskStates, blocking vs non-blocking
patterns.what: An agent responds to a message with either a stateless `Message` (trivial/transactional) or a stateful `Task`. `contextId` groups multiple Tasks and Messages into one conversation; `taskId` identifies one task. Exact `TaskState` enum values: `TASK_STATE_UNSPECIFIED`, `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED`, `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_FAILED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_CANCELED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_REJECTED` (terminal), `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` (interrupted), `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` (interrupted). SendMessageConfiguration.returnImmediately controls execution mode: false/unset = blocking, the call MUST wait until a terminal or interrupted state and return the latest state with all artifacts; true = return immediately after task creation and the caller polls (GetTask), subscribes (SubscribeToTask), or relies on push notifications. Sending a message to a task in a terminal state is UnsupportedOperationError. Tasks are immutable in the sense that refinements produce new artifacts/versions rather than mutating prior ones; artifacts are referenced and tracked by artifactId. v1.0 adds canonical errors via google.rpc.Status/ErrorInfo, ISO 8601 timestamps, cursor pagination on ListTasks (pageSize 1..100, default 50), and `A2A-Version` / `A2A-Extensions` HTTP headers.
patterns.why: This is the state machine the cockpit must render. hermes-day's sections (In flight / Needs you / Finished) map almost one-to-one onto WORKING / INPUT_REQUIRED+AUTH_REQUIRED / terminal — and INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED are exactly the 'waiting on you' kinds the whole plugin exists to surface. Getting blocking-vs-non-blocking right also decides whether a remote agent can hang a turn.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `A2ATask{task_id, context_id, state, status_message, artifacts[], timestamp}` with a strict state->section mapping: WORKING/SUBMITTED -> in-flight, INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED -> needs-you (AUTH_REQUIRED gets an auth card, not a question card), COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELED/REJECTED -> review queue. Always send `returnImmediately: true` from the cockpit (never let a UI action block on a remote agent) and drive updates via SubscribeToTask; keep a blocking path only for explicit one-shot calls. Parse google.rpc.Status errors into {code, message, details} and render the canonical code, not a raw string. Send `A2A-Version` on every request.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_task.py — assert each of the eight states lands in exactly one cockpit section (table-driven, including UNSPECIFIED which must not silently look like WORKING); that AUTH_REQUIRED produces an auth card and not a question card; that a message sent to a COMPLETED task surfaces UnsupportedOperationError; that a non-blocking send returns within the timeout with no artifacts; and that a google.rpc.Status error renders its canonical code.

patterns.name: A2A streaming: SSE of TaskStatusUpdateEvent / TaskArtifactUpdateEvent with final-chunk semantics
patterns.what: SendStreamingMessage (formerly message/stream) returns a StreamResponse: an initial Task OR Message, then a stream of TaskStatusUpdateEvent {taskId, contextId, status{state, message?, timestamp}, metadata?} and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent {taskId, contextId, artifact, append?, lastChunk?, metadata?} (spec sections 3.1.2, 3.2.3, 4.2). `append:true` means the artifact content should be appended to a previously sent artifact with the same artifactId; `lastChunk:true` marks the final chunk of that artifact. The stream carries a final completion indicator. Streaming unsupported by the agent -> UnsupportedOperationError (check `agentCard.capabilities.streaming` first — capability validation is required). SubscribeToTask (formerly tasks/resubscribe) re-attaches to an existing task's stream, which is how a reconnecting cockpit recovers a task it lost track of.
patterns.why: Artifact chunking with append/lastChunk is the exact mechanism hermes-day needs to stream a remote agent's partial output into a card the way it already streams local session output — and SubscribeToTask is the reconnect story for a cockpit that closes and reopens. Without append/lastChunk handling a long artifact renders as N disconnected blobs.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `A2AStreamConsumer` — asserts `capabilities.streaming` before calling; maintains an artifactId -> buffer map; on append:true concatenates, on lastChunk:true seals and emits one finished artifact. Status updates mutate the task's section in place (never append a new row per update). On stream drop, re-attach via SubscribeToTask and reconcile by taskId+artifactId rather than restarting. Desktop: in-flight cards render the live artifact buffer with a chunk counter; a sealed artifact moves to the review queue.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_stream.py — fixture stream emitting 3 artifact chunks (2 append:true, then lastChunk:true) interleaved with 4 status updates. Assert exactly one artifact is produced (not 3), that 4 status updates cause 1 card mutation and 0 new rows, that calling stream without `capabilities.streaming` never issues the RPC, and that a mid-stream drop + SubscribeToTask reconciles to the same artifactId without duplicating content.

patterns.name: A2A push notifications: TaskPushNotificationConfig + webhook auth (JWT/JWKS)
patterns.what: When the client is offline the agent POSTs to a registered webhook (spec section 4.3, Push Notification Objects). TaskPushNotificationConfig = {tenant?, id?, taskId?, url (required), token?, authentication?{scheme, credentials?}}. The notification is an HTTP POST to `url` with `Content-Type: application/a2a+json` and an `Authorization: {scheme} {credentials}` header, and the body is a StreamResponse containing exactly one of task | message | statusUpdate | artifactUpdate — i.e. push carries the same event types as the SSE stream. Config CRUD: CreatePushNotificationConfig / GetPushNotificationConfig / ListPushNotificationConfigs / DeletePushNotificationConfig. Server-side security: don't leak tokens, protect webhook URLs, validate the client webhook. Receiver-side: validate the source, use allowlists, verify signed tokens. Recommended flow is an asymmetric JWT: the agent signs with its private key including iss/aud/iat/exp/jti/taskId, publishes JWKS, and the webhook verifies the signature and claims; reject stale notifications by timestamp and dedupe by jti/event id.
patterns.why: This is the mechanism that makes hermes-day's promise ('what finished while you weren't looking') hold for remote agents, not just local sessions. It is also the highest-risk surface in the whole cluster: an unauthenticated webhook is a remote code-shaped hole, and the JWT/JWKS flow is precisely what the harness must implement rather than hand-wave.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: `PushNotificationReceiver` — HTTP endpoint with a per-config shared token, JWT verification against a cached JWKS (with key rotation), claim validation (iss/aud/iat/exp/jti), timestamp freshness window, and jti replay cache. Reject by default when `authentication` is absent and the server is not on a local allowlist. Register configs on task creation, delete on terminal state. Feed verified payloads into the same event pipeline as SSE (one consumer, two sources). Desktop: a push-notification badge per source showing last-verified-at and rejected count.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_push.py — assert (a) an unsigned POST is rejected, (b) a JWT signed by the wrong key is rejected, (c) an expired/nbf-violating JWT is rejected, (d) a replayed jti is rejected exactly once, (e) a valid notification mutates the same task card a stream would, and (f) no token or credential appears in logs.

patterns.name: A2A v1.0 wire contract: PascalCase methods, unified Part, discriminator stream events, A2A-Version
patterns.what: v1.0 renames JSON-RPC methods from lowercase slash form to PascalCase: message/send -> SendMessage, message/stream -> SendStreamingMessage, tasks/get -> GetTask, tasks/list -> ListTasks, tasks/cancel -> CancelTask, tasks/resubscribe -> SubscribeToTask, plus the four push-notification-config operations and GetExtendedAgentCard. Part is unified into a single object with OneOf {text, raw(base64), url, data} plus optional metadata/filename (previously separate TextPart/FilePart/DataPart — CRITICAL breaking change). Stream events adopt a discriminator pattern instead of a union that must be sniffed. AgentCard restructured (capabilities.streaming / pushNotifications / extendedAgentCard all under AgentCapabilities). Errors standardized on google.rpc.Status/ErrorInfo. Timestamps ISO 8601. Pagination is cursor-based (pageToken/next_page_token). Two HTTP headers are registered: `A2A-Version` and `A2A-Extensions`; media type is `application/a2a+json`; a well-known URI is registered for the card. Clients SHOULD send A2A-Version and negotiate; SDKs are expected to support multiple versions during migration.
patterns.why: Without this, an adapter written against v0.3.0 wire shapes fails against a v1.0 agent in ways that look like corruption rather than version skew. The unified Part and discriminator changes are exactly the kind of thing a harness must encode once, centrally, or rediscover in every adapter. A2A-Version + A2A-Extensions is also the same negotiation idea as MCP's extensions map — worth sharing one implementation.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: a `Part` normalizer handling all four OneOf arms (raw -> base64 decode to bytes with size guard, url -> deferred fetch, data -> structured), a stream-event discriminator switch (exhaustive, with an explicit unknown-variant branch that logs rather than crashes), and a shared `negotiate_headers()` used by both the MCP and A2A clients to emit version + extensions headers. Never sniff a stream event's shape by key presence; switch on the discriminator. Add a compatibility test fixture set for both v0.3.0 and v1.0 payloads.
patterns.test: tests/test_protocols_a2a_wire.py — assert all four Part arms normalize (including a 10MB raw part being refused rather than loaded), that an unknown stream discriminator logs and skips instead of raising, that A2A-Version and A2A-Extensions are present on every request, that Content-Type is application/a2a+json, and that a v0.3.0-shaped payload is detected and reported as version skew with an actionable message.

patterns.name: AG-UI event stream: the typed event catalogue and its flow patterns
patterns.what: A streaming, typed event protocol. Base properties on every event: type, optional timestamp, optional rawEvent, optional metadata. Categories and members: Lifecycle (RUN_STARTED, RUN_FINISHED, RUN_ERROR, STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED); Text messages (TEXT_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END, plus a TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK shorthand); Tool calls (TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END/RESULT, plus TOOL_CALL_CHUNK); State (STATE_SNAPSHOT, STATE_DELTA, MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT); Activity (ACTIVITY_SNAPSHOT, ACTIVITY_DELTA); Reasoning (REASONING_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END/CHUNK, REASONING_END, REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE); Subagent (SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED/ERROR); Special (RAW, CUSTOM); drafts (MetaEvent). Three canonical flow patterns: Start-Content-End (streaming content), Snapshot-Delta (state sync), Started/Finished|Error (lifecycle). Events should be processed in receipt order; events sharing an id (messageId, toolCallId) belong to one logical stream; implementations should be resilient to out-of-order delivery. Transport-agnostic (SSE, WebSockets, webhooks) and the agent interface is `run(input: RunAgentInput) -> Observable<BaseEvent>`.
patterns.why: AG-UI is the surface-facing protocol of the trio (MCP = agent->tools, A2A = agent->agent, AG-UI = agent->user). hermes-day's cockpit is exactly an AG-UI-shaped consumer: it renders run progress, tool calls, and state. Adopting the event catalogue gives the plugin a provider-neutral internal event bus and makes the cockpit drivable by any AG-UI agent, not just Hermes sessions.
patterns.build: `hday_events.py` (new): an internal `CockpitEvent` union mirroring the AG-UI catalogue (lifecycle/text/tool/state/activity/reasoning/subagent/custom) with a single `reduce(state, event)` reducer, plus adapters Hermes-hook -> CockpitEvent (agent_loop_stopped -> RUN_FINISHED, subagent_start/stop -> SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED, pre_tool_call/post_tool_call -> TOOL_CALL_START/END) and CockpitEvent -> AG-UI wire (so hermes-day can serve its own state to an AG-UI client). The reducer is pure and order-tolerant: a TOOL_CALL_ARGS for an unknown toolCallId opens an implicit START rather than dropping the event. Desktop: plugin.js subscribes to the reducer's output instead of ad-hoc hook payloads.
patterns.test: tests/test_events_reducer.py — golden-stream tests: feed a recorded event sequence and assert the reduced cockpit state; feed the same sequence shuffled within a messageId group and assert the same final state; feed a TOOL_CALL_ARGS with no START and assert an implicit start; assert every AG-UI event type maps to exactly one CockpitEvent variant (no silent drops) with an explicit `unmapped` counter that the test asserts is zero.

patterns.name: AG-UI shared state: STATE_SNAPSHOT + STATE_DELTA (RFC 6902 JSON Patch) and the two-way channel
patterns.what: State is a structured object that persists across interactions, is readable by both agent and frontend, and is mutable from both sides. Two sync methods: STATE_SNAPSHOT {type, snapshot} delivers a complete state and the frontend must REPLACE its model entirely; STATE_DELTA {type, delta: JsonPatchOperation[]} carries RFC 6902 ops ({op: add|remove|replace|move|copy|test, path: JSON Pointer (RFC 6901), value?, from?}) to be applied in sequence. Snapshots are for establishing a baseline, post-interruption resync, and major changes; deltas for high-frequency small updates. The reference implementation applies patches with fast-json-patch non-mutatingly and catches failures (logging state + patch) rather than corrupting state; if inconsistency is detected the frontend can request a fresh STATE_SNAPSHOT. MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT carries the complete conversation history. State is run-scoped. Best practices include explicit conflict resolution between agent and frontend writes and never storing sensitive data in shared state.
patterns.why: This is the mechanism that lets the cockpit and the agent share one model of the day — the agent can write 'these three items are snoozed' and the UI can write 'user muted this source' into the same object. Delta-with-snapshot-fallback is also the only bandwidth-sane way to keep a long-lived cockpit board in sync over a remote connection.
patterns.build: `hday_state.py` (new): a `SharedDayState` document (queues, mutes, pins, focus mode, filters) with `apply_snapshot`, `apply_delta` (RFC 6902, applied non-mutatingly, all-or-nothing, failure logged with the full patch), and `request_resync()` on detected inconsistency. Both the Python hook layer and `desktop/plugin.js` read/write it; UI writes emit deltas that are also sent to the agent. Conflict policy: user-authored keys (mutes, pins) are UI-authoritative and agent writes to them are rejected with a logged warning; agent-authored keys (summaries, derived badges) are agent-authoritative. Sensitive fields (tokens, session content) are excluded from the shared document by an explicit allowlist.
patterns.test: tests/test_state_patch.py — assert snapshot fully replaces prior state (no merge residue); that a delta whose 3rd op is invalid leaves state byte-identical to before (all-or-nothing); that applying a valid sequence of 200 ops yields the same result as the equivalent snapshot; that an agent write to a UI-authoritative key is rejected and logged; and that no allowlisted-out field ever appears in the serialized shared state.

patterns.name: AG-UI interrupts: RunFinished outcome=interrupt, the Interrupt type, and resume
patterns.what: Runs are interrupt-aware: RunFinishedEvent gains an optional `outcome` discriminated union — omitted (legacy, treat as normal completion), {type:'success'}, or {type:'interrupt', interrupts:[...]} where interrupts is non-empty. Interrupt = {id, reason, message?, toolCallId?, responseSchema?, expiresAt?, metadata?, subagentRunId?} — id is the correlation key across interrupt/resume/idempotency/audit; reason is a categorical routing hint (core values plus custom); responseSchema is a JSON Schema for the expected resume.payload; expiresAt is an ISO-8601 TTL and stale resumes produce RunError; subagentRunId attributes an interrupt raised inside a subagent. Resume: the next RunAgentInput on the SAME threadId carries `resume: [{interruptId, status:'resolved'|'cancelled', payload?, metadata?}]`. Denials are expressed INSIDE the payload (e.g. {approved:false}), not as a separate status. metadata carries envelope data (e.g. a signature proving the human decision wasn't tampered with) and reserves the `ag-ui` key. Contract rules: same threadId; resume[].interruptId must reference an id from the interrupted run; the resume array must address EVERY open interrupt (partial resumes unsupported). RunStarted also gains optional parentRunId (branching/time travel) and input (exact agent input for the run).
patterns.why: This is the single closest protocol match to hermes-day's raison d'être. The cockpit IS an interrupt-resolution surface: 'Needs you' is a list of open interrupts, and the approve-with-edits / deny-with-reason flows are exactly the resolved-with-payload semantics. Adopting the AG-UI interrupt shape makes hermes-day's approvals portable and makes its audit trail cryptographically attestable via the metadata envelope.
patterns.build: `hday_interrupts.py` (new): `Interrupt{id, reason, message, tool_call_id, response_schema, expires_at, metadata, subagent_run_id}` with a reason taxonomy mapped to cockpit kinds (tool_call -> approval card, input_required -> question card, custom -> generic). The cockpit's a/d/s/o keys produce resume entries: `a` -> {status:'resolved', payload:{approved:true}}, `d` -> {status:'resolved', payload:{approved:false, reason:...}} (denial inside payload), `s` -> no resume, snooze locally and re-surface. Enforce all three contract rules in code: thread match, interruptId linkage, and complete coverage of the open set — a partial submit is rejected client-side before any RPC. Reject resumes past expiresAt with a RunError rather than a silent no-op. Sign the metadata envelope with the profile key so an approval is attributable.
patterns.test: tests/test_interrupts_resume.py — assert (a) a legacy RunFinished with no outcome is treated as success, (b) a partial resume addressing 2 of 3 open interrupts is refused client-side, (c) resume[].interruptId not present in the interrupted run is refused, (d) a resume on a different threadId is refused, (e) a denial round-trips as payload{approved:false} and never as status:'cancelled', (f) an expired interrupt yields RunError and clears pending state, (g) the metadata signature verifies and a tampered payload fails.

patterns.name: AG-UI capability discovery: getCapabilities() and feature gating
patterns.what: AbstractAgent exposes an optional `getCapabilities(): Promise<AgentCapabilities>` returning a typed snapshot of what the agent currently supports. Principles: discovery only (no negotiation), dynamic (reflects current state), optional (agents that don't implement it return undefined), and absent-means-unknown (only declare what you support). AgentCapabilities categories: identity {name, type, description, version, provider, documentationUrl, metadata}, transport {streaming, websocket, httpBinary, pushNotifications, resumable}, tools {supported, items, clientProvided}, output {structuredOutput, mimeTypes}, state {snapshots, deltas, persistence}, multiAgent {delegation, handoffs, subagents}, reasoning {supported, encrypted thinking}, multimodal (by direction), execution {code execution, timeouts, iteration caps}, humanInTheLoop {approvals, interventions, feedback, interrupts, approveWithEdits}, and a `custom` escape hatch. Clients use it for adaptive UI and feature gating, and must gate on explicit equality (capabilities?.output?.structuredOutput === true) because an omitted field means undeclared, not unsupported.
patterns.why: hermes-day renders across desktop, TUI, and Discord — three surfaces with different capabilities. AG-UI's capability model is the cleanest available vocabulary for 'what can this surface/agent actually do', and the absent-means-unknown rule is the exact discipline that stops the cockpit from rendering an affordance it can't honour. It also gives hermes-day a principled way to declare its own capabilities to a connecting client.
patterns.build: `hday_protocols.py`: an `AgentCapabilities` dataclass set mirroring the AG-UI categories, implemented per surface (desktop / TUI / Discord) and per connected agent, with `get_capabilities()` on both sides. `desktop/plugin.js` gates every affordance on explicit truthiness (never on falsiness of an omitted field): no approval UI unless humanInTheLoop.approvals === true, no reasoning panel unless reasoning.supported === true, no live artifact streaming unless transport.streaming === true. `custom` carries hermes-day specifics (e.g. {'com.hermes-day/surfaces': [...]}). Serve the capability document over the same AG-UI endpoint the event stream uses.
patterns.test: tests/test_capabilities_gating.py — assert an omitted field and an explicit false behave identically for gating (both hide the affordance); that a capability added at runtime is reflected on the next call; that each surface declares a distinct transport set; and that a client asking for structured output when the agent's output.structuredOutput is absent falls back to text rather than erroring.

patterns.name: AG-UI subagents: subagentRunId attribution and suspension
patterns.what: AG-UI does NOT orchestrate subagents — it only attributes events to the subagent that produced them. Three events: SubagentStarted {subagentRunId (required), name (required), description?, parentSubagentRunId?, parentToolCallId?, parentMessageId?}, SubagentFinished {subagentRunId, result?, outcome? {type:'success'} | {type:'suspended', interruptIds?[]}}, SubagentError. `subagentRunId` is an opaque handle for ONE INVOCATION (like runId), never a reusable definition — use `name` for 'which kind of subagent'. The one exception: a subagent that finished with outcome {type:'suspended'} MAY reuse its id on a resuming run, and the client must treat that later SubagentStarted as a continuation (waiting -> running), never as a duplicate. Every started subagent closes before RunFinished; a paused subagent emits SubagentFinished with outcome 'suspended' so the UI can render 'waiting' not 'done'. Attribution transfers to messages and tool results, which carry their own attribution. parentToolCallId/parentMessageId exist for the agents-as-tools pattern so the subagent's output can render inside the tool-call card. A version shim strips subagent fields in both directions against older peers, which flattens attribution. Known limits: protobuf covers 19 of 36 event types; .NET loses the second owner on parallel tool calls from different subagents.
patterns.why: hermes-day already has subagent_start / subagent_stop hooks but no attribution model — so three concurrent subagents currently render as one undifferentiated stream in the cockpit. This is the exact problem AG-UI's subagent spec solves, and the invocation-vs-definition distinction is the trap that would otherwise cause the cockpit to persist state under a meaningless key.
patterns.build: `hday_events.py`: map Hermes subagent_start/stop into SUBAGENT_STARTED/FINISHED with a freshly minted `subagentRunId` (never the profile or agent name), keeping `name` for display. Key all transient UI state (spinner, collapsible group, progress row) by subagentRunId and persist NOTHING by it. Implement the suspension rule: a subagent that paused on an approval emits outcome {type:'suspended', interruptIds:[...]} and the cockpit renders 'waiting'; a later SUBAGENT_STARTED with the same id is a continuation, not a duplicate row. Desktop: group cards by parentToolCallId when present so an agents-as-tools subagent nests inside its tool card.
patterns.test: tests/test_subagents_attribution.py — assert two invocations of the same-named subagent get distinct subagentRunIds and produce two rows; that a suspended subagent renders 'waiting' and not 'done'; that a resumed SUBAGENT_STARTED with a reused id updates the existing row instead of creating a second; that no UI state is persisted keyed by subagentRunId; and that output from a nested subagent lands inside its parentToolCallId card.

patterns.name: CopilotKit: useAgent + useAgentContext as the two-way shared-state client
patterns.what: `useAgent(options?) -> {agent: AbstractAgent, isReady: boolean}` returns a live AG-UI AbstractAgent and re-renders on state/message/status change. Exactly two option shapes are valid: bind to the shared registry instance ({agentId} or nothing), or bind a PRIVATE agent to a thread — all three of {agentId, runtimeAgentId, threadId} required; partial combinations are type errors (a runtime agent registered under an id is a singleton, so a per-hook threadId on it would let two hooks clobber each other). `updates: [UseAgentUpdate.OnStateChanged | OnMessagesChanged]` throttles re-renders. `agent.state` is plain data; `agent.setState({...})` writes back and the agent reads it on its next turn. `isReady` is false while the runtime connects, with `agent` being a fully-constructed provisional stand-in — guard one-time subscriptions on isReady. `agent.subscribe({onRunStartedEvent, onRunFinalized})` returns `{unsubscribe}`. `useAgentContext` is the one-way, UI-owned, auto-unregistering read-only channel (current user, selected record, scroll position) for values the agent should read but never write. Server side, `CopilotKitMiddleware` picks up CopilotKit state alongside the app's own; `copilotkit_emit_state` pushes state to the frontend; `StateStreamingMiddleware(StateItem(state_key=..., tool=..., tool_argument=...))` streams a tool argument token-by-token into state[key] while the call is still in flight — and the frontend's subscription indexes partial-JSON-parsed args by `state_key`, so the tool argument name MUST equal state_key. The older `useCoAgent` name now resolves to `useAgent`.
patterns.why: This is the concrete client-side recipe for the AG-UI shared-state pattern above, and the two footguns it documents (singleton runtime agent vs per-thread private agent; tool-argument-name-must-equal-state_key) are exactly the bugs a hermes-day implementation would hit. useAgentContext is also the right home for hermes-day's read-only signals (active profile, focused pane, current filter) — values the agent should see but never overwrite.
patterns.build: In `desktop/plugin.js`: use the thread-scoped form ({agentId: `day-${threadId}`, runtimeAgentId: 'default', threadId}) so multiple cockpit panes against one runtime agent don't clobber threads; subscribe with `updates: [UseAgentUpdate.OnStateChanged]` to avoid re-render storms on a board with many rows; guard the one-time interrupt subscription on `isReady`. Publish read-only cockpit context (active profile, focused pane, filter text, mute set) through the useAgentContext equivalent (the plugin's context-registration API) rather than writing it into shared state. On the Python side, mirror StateStreamingMiddleware for hermes-day's long-running evidence runs so a partial test log streams into state['evidence'] as it is produced, with the tool argument named `evidence`.
patterns.test: tests/test_copilotkit_bindings.py + a node:vm plugin.js harness — assert partial option combinations are rejected (type-level and runtime), that a board with 200 rows and OnStateChanged-only subscription re-renders once per state change rather than per message, that a subscription registered before isReady does not bind to the provisional agent, and that a streamed tool argument lands under state[key] exactly when the argument name equals state_key and never otherwise.

patterns.name: CopilotKit HITL hooks: useHumanInTheLoop (interactive tool) and useInterrupt (AG-UI standard interrupts)
patterns.what: Two distinct HITL mechanisms. (1) useHumanInTheLoop(tool, deps?) registers an interactive tool with NO handler: an internal status machine (ToolCallStatus.InProgress -> Executing -> Complete) supplies a `respond` callback to the render component during Executing, and the agent stays paused until respond(value) is called — exactly once per invocation. Built on useFrontendTool; registered on mount, removed on unmount; returns void. (2) useInterrupt(config) handles agent interrupts and resumes execution. It supports the AG-UI standard flow (RUN_FINISHED with outcome.type === 'interrupt' carrying interrupts[]) AND the legacy custom-event flow (`on_interrupt`), with standard taking precedence when both appear in one run. Callbacks receive `interrupt` (the primary) and `interrupts` (the full open set); `resolve(payload)` resumes, `cancel()` cancels; responses accumulate one per open interrupt and the resume run starts only once every open interrupt is addressed. Expired interrupts (past expiresAt) are NOT resumed — the hook logs an error and clears pending state. Interrupt UI renders inside <CopilotChat> by default; `renderInChat:false` returns the element for manual placement. Starting a new run clears pending interrupt state. `event.value` is typed any and must be narrowed.
patterns.why: These two are the difference between a cockpit that can only *show* a pending approval and one that can *answer* it. The status-machine contract (pause on Executing, respond once) is what keeps a board honest under double-clicks, and useInterrupt's 'resume only when every open interrupt is addressed' rule is the same completeness constraint the cockpit must enforce across parallel approvals from different subagents.
patterns.build: In `desktop/plugin.js`: the approval card is a useHumanInTheLoop-shaped component — while status is Executing the card shows a/d buttons and `respond` is called exactly once (disable after first call); after Complete the card renders the recorded result inline. Wrap the whole board in a useInterrupt-shaped handler so interrupts raised anywhere (including inside subagents, via subagentRunId) surface in 'Needs you' with a resolve/cancel pair, and hold the resume until the open set is fully addressed. Treat an expired interrupt as a distinct visual state ('expired — re-ask') that never silently resumes. Keep the legacy on_interrupt path behind a capability check for older agents.
patterns.test: tests/test_copilotkit_hitl.py + plugin.js harness — assert respond is callable once and a second call is a no-op; that the agent stays paused (no resume emitted) until respond fires; that resolve() on 2 of 3 open interrupts emits no resume run; that cancel() on all open interrupts resumes with statuses 'cancelled'; that an expired interrupt logs and clears rather than resuming; and that a legacy on_interrupt event is handled when the standard outcome is absent but ignored when present.

patterns.name: Generative UI specs: A2UI surfaces/actions and MCP-UI iframes as the two renderable targets
patterns.what: AG-UI is explicitly NOT a generative-UI spec — it is the bidirectional runtime connection that carries one. Three sibling specs: A2UI (Google, declarative LLM-friendly, JSONL-based and streaming, platform-agnostic; current production release v0.9.1 standardizing on `application/a2ui+json`, v1.0 candidate adds client-to-server RPC (`actionResponse`), action IDs, and renames theme to surfaceProperties; v0.9 introduced `createSurface`, client-side functions, custom catalogs, and a prompt-first philosophy; renderers exist for Angular, Flutter, Lit, Markdown). MCP-UI (Microsoft + Shopify; iframe-based, extends MCP; client/server SDKs, 5.2k stars, Ruby/Python SDKs in progress). Open-JSON-UI (OpenAI, declarative). A2UI transports: A2A extension (stable), AG-UI (stable, CopilotKit is AG-UI's creator and primary consumer), REST/WebSockets/SSE proposed. A2UI's design rules: declarative data not executable code, agents may only use pre-approved components from the client's catalog (no UI injection), flat streaming JSON for incremental LLM generation, adjacency-list component model, data binding, and progressive rendering. AG-UI's own generative-UI draft proposes a two-step `generateUserInterface` tool ({description, data, output}) delegated to a secondary LLM, with documented limits: OpenAI's 1024-char tool-description cap, unreliable $ref/oneOf support across providers, and context-window pressure (dedicated UI agents outperform combined ones).
patterns.why: This is the cross-surface payoff: one declarative payload, rendered natively on desktop, TUI (as text/markdown), and Discord (as components). The catalog restriction is also the security model — agents can only compose components the client already trusts, which is the only generative-UI design compatible with hermes-day's existing stance on untrusted content.
patterns.build: `desktop/plugin.js`: an `a2ui` renderer implementing the adjacency-list model with a hermes-day catalog (card, table, diff, progress, chart, form, action-button) and `application/a2ui+json` ingestion from an AG-UI CUSTOM event or a tool result; an `mcp-ui` renderer reusing the sandboxed-iframe machinery from the MCP Apps pattern. A surface is a named container in the rail; `createSurface` and `actionResponse` (v1.0) drive client->server actions. TUI and Discord surfaces implement a degraded catalog (text/table/diff only) and declare that in capabilities — never silently render nothing. Route every generated-UI action through the gate with origin='genui'. Keep the catalog closed: an unknown component type renders as a labeled placeholder, never as raw HTML.
patterns.test: tests/test_genui_render.py + plugin.js harness — assert an unknown component type renders a placeholder and increments a counter (never raw HTML); that the same A2UI payload renders to a table on desktop, plain text on TUI, and a degraded form on Discord per each surface's declared catalog; that a surface action produces a gate record with origin='genui'; and that a payload missing a required component reference fails closed.

patterns.name: OTel GenAI: inference client spans and the content-capture contract
patterns.what: Moved out of the main semconv repo into open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai (the old opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/ pages are stubs pointing there; status Development). Span type `gen_ai.inference.client`: kind CLIENT (INTERNAL allowed for in-process models), span name `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`, and a span SHOULD cover the logical operation including automatic retries. Required attributes: `gen_ai.operation.name` (chat | generate_content | text_completion | embeddings | execute_tool | invoke_agent | invoke_workflow | plan | retrieval | fetch_response | create_agent | memory ops ...), `gen_ai.provider.name` (openai | gcp.gen_ai | aws.bedrock | ... — a discriminator selecting the provider-specific telemetry flavour). Conditionally required: error.type, gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.output.type, gen_ai.prompt.name/version, gen_ai.request.choice.count/model/seed/stream/top_k, server.port. Recommended: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, frequency/presence_penalty, stop_sequences, reasoning.level, response.id/model/finish_reasons, and `gen_ai.response.time_to_first_chunk` (seconds, streaming only). Content capture is opt-in and three-tiered: `gen_ai.system_instructions`, `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` follow fixed JSON schemas (model/gen-ai/gen-ai-input-messages.json, -output-messages.json, -system-instructions.json); they may be recorded structured on events, or JSON-serialized on spans where structured attributes aren't supported; instrumentations MAY expose an in-process hook that fires regardless of the sampling decision to upload content to external storage and enrich the span.
patterns.why: hermes-day's decision ledger currently records only Hermes-internal facts. OTel GenAI conventions are the only cross-provider vocabulary that lets the cockpit show cost/latency/model attribution uniformly across providers — and the time_to_first_chunk attribute plus the conversation.id correlation are exactly what a day-view needs to explain 'why did this turn feel slow'. The `gen_ai.provider.name` discriminator rule is also the correct way to keep provider-specific attributes from bleeding into each other.
patterns.build: `hday_telemetry.py` (new): emit OTel-shaped span records into the decision ledger alongside the existing entries — span name `{operation} {model}`, required attributes always present, provider-specific attributes namespaced under the provider prefix, and `gen_ai.conversation.id` set from the Hermes session id so a cockpit row can join telemetry to sessions. Content capture is OFF by default and gated behind an explicit config flag with a per-field truncation option that preserves JSON structure. Implement the upload hook as a no-op-by-default callable so a deployment can wire content to its own storage without changing the ledger schema.
patterns.test: tests/test_telemetry_genai.py — assert every emitted span carries gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.provider.name; that no content attribute is present when capture is disabled; that enabling truncation preserves JSON structure while shortening contents; that a retried request produces one span (not N); that time_to_first_chunk is emitted only for streaming requests; and that provider-specific attributes never appear on a span whose provider.name is a different provider.

patterns.name: OTel GenAI: agent/framework spans (create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan) and the execute_tool span
patterns.what: Agent conventions extend and override the inference conventions. `gen_ai.create_agent.client` (operation name create_agent, span name `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`, kind CLIENT) carries gen_ai.agent.id (a STABLE provider-assigned identifier — AWS Bedrock agent ARN, GCP Agent Registry identifier; in-memory instance ids are explicitly NOT recommended), gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.agent.description, gen_ai.agent.version, plus the usual model/server attributes. Other operation names: invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan (agent planning or task decomposition phase), retrieval, fetch_response (retrieve a prior response by id WITHOUT inference — and instrumentations SHOULD NOT report token usage for it). Agent spans support span creation-time attributes (gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.operation.name) so sampling decisions can be made on them. Tool execution uses the shared `execute_tool` span; MCP tool-call spans are explicitly compatible with it and an MCP instrumentation that detects outer GenAI tool tracing SHOULD NOT create a second span but add MCP attributes to the existing one.
patterns.why: hermes-day is multi-agent by construction (profiles, subagents, remote agents). These conventions are the vocabulary that lets the cockpit's per-agent rows carry a stable identity across runs — and the 'don't create a duplicate execute_tool span' rule is precisely the mistake a hook-based harness makes, since it already observes tool calls from two directions (Hermes hooks and MCP instrumentation).
patterns.build: `hday_telemetry.py`: emit create_agent / invoke_agent / invoke_workflow / plan spans for profile spawns, subagent dispatch, and mission plans, using gen_ai.agent.id = the stable profile/subagent-definition identifier and gen_ai.agent.name for display. Set agent.name and operation.name at span creation so sampling can use them. Add a dedupe guard: if a Hermes pre_tool_call span already exists for a given tool invocation, the MCP layer MUST annotate it rather than open a second execute_tool span (key on (server, jsonrpc_id) or (session, tool_call_id)). Never report token usage on fetch_response operations.
patterns.test: tests/test_telemetry_agent_spans.py — assert agent.id is the stable definition id and not a per-run instance id; that a tool call observed by both the Hermes hook layer and the MCP layer produces exactly one execute_tool span with both attribute sets; that fetch_response spans carry no usage attributes; and that agent.name/operation.name are present at span creation time.

patterns.name: OTel GenAI events + MCP semantic conventions: opt-in content events, context propagation via params._meta, and MCP metrics
patterns.what: Events: `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details` (opt-in, requirement level Opt-In) carries the same attribute set as inference spans including chat history and parameters, and exists so input/output details can be stored independently of traces; `gen_ai.evaluation.result` carries gen_ai.evaluation.name (required), score.value, score.label, explanation, and gen_ai.response.id. MCP conventions (RECOMMENDED over generic RPC/HTTP conventions, because one HTTP request can carry multiple MCP messages and one streamable-HTTP request can serve several): context propagation by injecting W3C Trace Context into the MCP request `params._meta` property bag — keys `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `baggage` written UNPREFIXED even though `_meta` keys are normally DNS-prefixed (SEP-414 defines this explicit exception); the receiver extracts from `params._meta` and uses it as the remote parent, linking (not parenting) ambient HTTP context, since MCP and transport contexts are independent. MCP spans: kind CLIENT, name `{mcp.method.name} {target}` where target matches gen_ai.tool.name or gen_ai.prompt.name (resource URIs only on opt-in, to avoid cardinality), with attributes mcp.method.name (required), mcp.protocol.version, mcp.session.id, mcp.resource.uri, jsonrpc.request.id, rpc.response.status_code, network.protocol.*. Metrics: mcp.client.operation.duration, mcp.server.operation.duration, mcp.client.session.duration, mcp.server.session.duration.
patterns.why: Two things hermes-day needs and cannot get from its own hooks: a trace context that survives a hop into an MCP server (so a cockpit row can link to the server-side span), and per-operation MCP duration metrics (so the Sources panel can show which server is slow rather than just 'errored'). The unprefixed `traceparent` exception is a real interop trap — a naive implementation DNS-prefixes it and silently breaks propagation.
patterns.build: `hday_telemetry.py`: inject traceparent/tracestate/baggage UNPREFIXED into every MCP request's `params._meta`, and extract on the server side using `_meta` as remote parent with a span LINK (not parent) to the ambient HTTP context. Emit the four mcp.* metrics with mcp.method.name and mcp.session.id labels; the Sources panel renders p95 duration per server from them. Emit `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details` events (opt-in) so content can be shipped to a separate store without polluting the trace; emit `gen_ai.evaluation.result` for the honesty-guard verdicts (name='hermes-day.evidence', score.label in {verified, no_evidence, checks_failed, guard_violation}) so evidence quality is queryable alongside the traces.
patterns.test: tests/test_telemetry_mcp.py — assert traceparent is written unprefixed into params._meta (a DNS-prefixed key fails the test), that the server span's parent is the MCP client span and the HTTP span appears as a link, that all four mcp.* metrics are emitted with method name labels, that gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details is absent unless opted in, and that a guard violation emits gen_ai.evaluation.result with the expected label.

patterns.name: OpenAI Realtime event model: the session/conversation/response event grammar
patterns.what: A WebSocket (or WebRTC/SIP) event protocol where every message is a typed event with an explicit `type` string; the reference client dispatches them as `server.{event_name}` and `client.{event_name}` and exposes a raw `realtime.event` stream carrying {time (ISO), source ('client'|'server'), event}. Client events include session.update, input_audio_buffer.append/commit/clear, conversation.item.create, conversation.item.truncate, response.create, response.cancel, output_audio_buffer.clear. Server events include session.created (which echoes the server's default instructions when the client set none), conversation.item.created, conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed (with a usage object billed against the ASR model, not the realtime model), input_audio_buffer.speech_started / speech_stopped / committed / cleared / dtmf_event_received, response.* deltas, and rate_limits/error events. Session config is set ahead of or during the connection via session.update: instructions, voice, tools (type 'function' + JSON-Schema parameters), turn_detection ({type:'server_vad', prefix_padding_ms default 300, silence_duration_ms default 500, threshold default 0.5} or null to disable VAD), input_audio_transcription ({model:'whisper-1'}), max_output_tokens (1..4096 or 'inf'). Item types in the conversation cache are message | function_call | function_call_output, with delta carrying exactly one of audio (Int16Array), transcript (string), or arguments (string). Audio is pcm16 @ 24 kHz by default.
patterns.why: Voice is a surface, and hermes-day is a triage surface — 'read me what's waiting' is a natural cockpit affordance, as is hands-free approval. The event grammar is also instructive independent of audio: it is a mature example of the same Start/Delta/Completed discipline AG-UI uses, and its turn_detection/VAD configuration is the mechanism that decides whether a voice surface interrupts the agent mid-sentence.
patterns.build: `hday_voice.py` (new): a thin event router that normalizes Realtime events into the same CockpitEvent union as the AG-UI adapter (session.created -> session-ready, input_audio_buffer.speech_started -> user-interrupt, response.* -> assistant stream, function_call items -> TOOL_CALL_*). Voice approvals reuse the interrupt machinery: a spoken 'approve' resolves the same open interrupt the keyboard does, and the resume payload is identical. Configure turn_detection explicitly (never rely on defaults) and set max_output_tokens so a read-out of a long queue cannot run away. Keep the API key server-side; the desktop surface must never hold it (the reference client warns explicitly against browser-side keys).
patterns.test: tests/test_voice_event_router.py — assert each normalized event maps to exactly one CockpitEvent variant; that a spoken approval produces the same resume payload as the keyboard path (byte-identical); that turn_detection is always explicitly set in session.update; and that no API key is ever serialized into the plugin's client-side config.

patterns.name: OpenAI Realtime: interruption semantics and MCP-tool approval inside the session
patterns.what: Interruption: the reference client's cancelResponse(id, sampleCount) immediately ceases generation AND truncates the played item — removing all audio after sampleCount and clearing the text response — specifically so the model does not 'remember' content it generated ahead of where the user actually heard. Push-to-talk over WebSocket: set turn_detection null; on push down, response.cancel if a response is in flight and conversation.item.truncate to drop unplayed audio; on push up, input_audio_buffer.append, input_audio_buffer.commit, then response.create. Over WebRTC/SIP the input audio buffer must be explicitly cleared (input_audio_buffer.clear) and unplayed output dropped with output_audio_buffer.clear, which also truncates the conversation. MCP: the realtime API reference includes MCP-specific models (realtime_mcp_approval_request among the realtime resource models), i.e. MCP tool calls inside a realtime session carry an explicit approval step in the event model rather than executing silently.
patterns.why: Truncate-on-interrupt is a correctness rule, not a nicety: without it the agent's memory diverges from what the human experienced, which is the same class of bug as an approval recorded but never shown. And the presence of an MCP approval-request event in the Realtime model is the strongest evidence that approval-before-tool-execution is now a protocol-level expectation across surfaces — which is exactly hermes-day's gate.
patterns.build: `hday_voice.py`: implement truncation faithfully — on barge-in, cancel the response, truncate at the samples actually played, and record the truncated length in the ledger so the transcript the cockpit shows matches what the human heard. Any MCP tool call arriving inside a realtime session must raise an approval request that lands in 'Needs you' like any other interrupt; never auto-approve because the channel is voice. Desktop: a voice session is a source row with a distinct chip and the same a/d keyboard affordances.
patterns.test: tests/test_voice_interrupt.py — assert barge-in emits cancel + truncate with the played-sample count and not the full length; that the recorded transcript matches the truncated audio; that an MCP tool call inside a voice session creates a pending approval and is not executed; and that approving by voice and by keyboard produce identical resume payloads.

patterns.name: MCP Registry: server.json metadata, reverse-DNS namespaces, and the aggregator REST API
patterns.what: The official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers (preview; backed by Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, Microsoft). Metadata is stored as `server.json` (schema at github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry/blob/main/docs/reference/server-json/draft/server.schema.json) containing the unique server name (reverse-DNS form, e.g. `io.github.user/server-name`), where to locate the server (npm package name, remote URL), execution instructions (args, env vars), and discovery data (description, capabilities). Namespace authentication ties names to verified GitHub accounts or domains (GitHub, DNS, or HTTP challenges), so only the legitimate owner can publish under a namespace.
